content.text: The European Mercantile Rivalry, British Colonial Expansion, Regional Subjugation, and Administrative Policies of Governor-Generals and Viceroys

The transition of European trading corporations from commercial maritime monopolies into territorial sovereign entities in South Asia reshaped Indian political economy. The English East India Company systematically eliminated mercantile rivals (Portuguese, Dutch, French) and subordinated regional sovereign powers (Bengal, Mysore, Marathas, Nizam of Hyderabad, and the Northern Circars of Andhra) through military conquest, fiscal manipulation, and strategic subsidiary alliances.

content.text: 1. European Mercantile Advent and Inter-Imperial Rivalry

content.caption: Chronology and Commercial Strongholds of European Powers in India
headers: Primary Settlements & Factories in India & Andhra
rows: Portuguese (Estado da India)
Vasco da Gama (1498, Calicut), Francisco de Almeida (Blue Water Policy), Afonso de Albuquerque (captured Goa in 1510).
Goa, Daman, Diu, Cochin; coastal settlements at San Thome (Madras) and Machilipatnam (Andhra).
Religious intolerance (Goa Inquisition), piracy, loss of naval supremacy to the Dutch and English (Battle of Swally Hole, 1612).
Dutch East India Company (VOC)
Formed in 1602; prioritized Spice Islands (Indonesia).
First factory established at Machilipatnam (1605, Andhra), Pulicat (headquarters until 1690), Nagapattinam, Chinsurah (Bengal).
Decisively defeated by the English at the Battle of Bedara/Chinsurah (1759) and by Marthanda Varma of Travancore at the Battle of Colachel (1741).
French East India Company
Colbert (1664); Francois Martin founded Pondicherry (1674); Joseph Francois Dupleix.
Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahe, Karaikal; factory at Machilipatnam and Yanam (Andhra).
Carnatic Wars (1746–1763); decisive defeat at Battle of Wandiwash (1760) by Sir Eyre Coote relegated French to commercial enclaves without military forts.
English East India Company (EIC)
Royal Charter from Queen Elizabeth I (1600); Captain William Hawkins and Sir Thomas Roe visited Jahangir's court.
First south Indian factory at Machilipatnam (1611); Surat (1612); Fort St. George in Madras (1639, Francis Day); Bombay (1668, dowry from Charles II); Fort William in Calcutta (1696, Job Charnock).
Emerged as the supreme imperial conqueror following Carnatic and Bengal victories.

content.text: 2. Colonial Conquest of Regional Kingdoms: Bengal, Mysore, Nizam & Andhra

content.caption: British Imperial Subjugation of Indian Regional Powers
rows: Bengal: Plassey & Buxar

Battle of Plassey (1757, Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah via betrayal of Mir Jafar); Battle of Buxar (1764, Hector Munro defeated combined armies of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula, and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II).

Treaty of Allahabad (1765) granted Diwani (fiscal revenue collection rights) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the EIC; established Robert Clive's predatory 'Dual Government' (1765–1772) inducing the Great Bengal Famine of 1770.
Mysore: Hyder Ali & Tipu Sultan
Four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–1799); Treaty of Seringapatam (1792); Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799).

Tipu Sultan resisted via modern French-assisted military, rocketry (Mysorean rockets), and diplomatic missions to Ottoman Turkey and France; fell defending Seringapatam (1799); Mysore reduced to subsidiary state under the Wodeyars.
Nizam of Hyderabad & The Northern Circars (Andhra)
Treaty of 1766 with Nizam Ali Khan; Subsidiary Alliance of 1798.

EIC secured the Northern Circars (Chicacole, Rajahmundry, Ellore, Mustafanagar, Kondaveedu) from the French (Bussy) and Nizam; Nizam became the first Indian prince to accept Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance in 1798; Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema: Bellary, Anantapur, Cuddapah, Kurnool) handed to EIC in 1800 to maintain British subsidiary troops.
Maratha Confederacy
Three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818); Treaty of Salbai (1782), Treaty of Bassein (1802).
Internal factionalism among Peshwa, Scindia, Holkar, Gaekwad, and Bhonsle exploited; Peshwaship abolished in 1818; Baji Rao II exiled to Bithur.

content.text: 3. Landmark Policies of Governor-Generals and Viceroys

content.caption: Administrative Milestones of British Governors-General and Viceroys
headers: Key Administrative, Revenue, Judicial & Political Enactments
rows: Warren Hastings

First Governor-General of Bengal; Regulating Act of 1773 (established Supreme Court at Calcutta); abolished Dual Government; founded Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784, William Jones); impeached in British Parliament.
Lord Cornwallis

'Father of the Civil Services in India'; Cornwallis Code (separation of revenue and judicial powers); Permanent Settlement of Bengal (Zamindari system, 1793) fixing state revenue demand perpetually with Sunset Law.
Lord Wellesley

Institutionalized Subsidiary Alliance system (forcing Indian states to disband standing armies, house British troops, expel other Europeans, and submit foreign relations to the British Resident); established Fort William College.
Lord William Bentinck

First Governor-General of India (Charter Act of 1833); abolished Sati (Regulation XVII of 1829); suppressed Thuggee (assisted by William Sleeman); English Education Act of 1835 based on Macaulay's Minute.
Lord Dalhousie

Doctrine of Lapse (annexed Satara, Sambalpur, Jhansi, Nagpur); annexed Awadh (1856) on charges of maladministration; introduced Railways (Bombay to Thane, 1853), Electric Telegraph, Postal Stamp reforms (1854), Wood's Despatch (1854), and Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856.
Lord Canning
Last Governor-General of EIC and First Viceroy of India under Government of India Act 1858 (Crown Rule); oversaw Indian Penal Code (IPC 1860) and Indian High Courts Act (1861).
Lord Ripon

'Father of Local Self-Government in India' (Resolution of 1882); repealed Vernacular Press Act (1882); First Factory Act of 1881; Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883) exposing racial discrimination in colonial judicial administration.
Lord Curzon
Partition of Bengal (1905) igniting the Swadeshi Movement; Indian Universities Act (1904); Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904); established Archaeological Survey of India (ASI).

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Explain the strategic mechanisms of Lord Wellesley's 'Subsidiary Alliance' and Lord Dalhousie's 'Doctrine of Lapse'. How did these imperial policies dismantle the sovereignty of Indian princely states? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Detail Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance: disarmament of the native state, stationing of a British subsidiary force maintained at the ruler's expense (or territorial cessions like Ceded Districts of Andhra), surrender of external foreign diplomacy, posting of an interfering British Resident, and first signatory (Nizam of Hyderabad, 1798); analyze Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse: refusal to recognize adopted heirs as natural successors to political sovereignty in dependent states, annexations (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur); evaluate how these twin legalistic doctrines systematically destabilized the traditional political order, culminating directly in the 1857 upheaval.

Trace the trajectory of the English East India Company's struggle for supremacy in the Coromandel coast and Northern Circars of Andhra. How did the Nizam of Hyderabad's territorial cessions shape modern Andhra Pradesh? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Detail early commercial factories at Machilipatnam (1611); analyze the Anglo-French rivalry in the Deccan during the Carnatic Wars (Dupleix vs. Clive, Bussy's influence at Hyderabad court); explain the Treaty of 1766 wherein Nizam Ali Khan surrendered the Northern Circars (Srikakulam, Rajahmundry, Eluru, Guntur) to the British in exchange for military protection; explain the 1800 Subsidiary Treaty whereby Nizam ceded the Rayalaseema districts (Ceded Districts / Datta Mandalam: Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur, Bellary) to fund subsidiary troops, establishing the administrative foundation of coastal and Rayalaseema regions under the Madras Presidency.

Critically evaluate the administrative and social reforms of Lord William Bentinck and Lord Ripon. Why is Ripon remembered as the most liberal Viceroy of British India? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Evaluate Bentinck's tenure: humanistic social legislation (Abolition of Sati 1829, suppression of female infanticide and Thuggee), judicial reorganization, and Macaulay's educational reforms (1835); evaluate Ripon's liberal administration: Resolution on Local Self-Government (1882) creating taluk and district boards with elected non-official chairpersons, repeal of the oppressive Vernacular Press Act, Factory Act (1881) regulating child labor, and his courageous stance on the Ilbert Bill (1883) granting Indian judges parity to try Europeans.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Which Indian ruler was the very first to accept the Subsidiary Alliance system formulated by Lord Wellesley in 1798?
(a) Nawab of Awadh
(b) Nizam of Hyderabad
(c) Peshwa Baji Rao II
(d) Raja of Tanjore
Correct Answer: (b) Nizam of Hyderabad [Explanation: Nizam Ali Khan of Hyderabad was the first Indian monarch to sign the Subsidiary Alliance treaty with Lord Wellesley in 1798.]

Q2. The Treaty of Allahabad (1765), which granted the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the British East India Company, was signed by Robert Clive and which Mughal Emperor?
(a) Farrukhsiyar
(b) Muhammad Shah Rangila
(c) Shah Alam II
(d) Bahadur Shah I
Correct Answer: (c) Shah Alam II [Explanation: Following the decisive victory in the Battle of Buxar (1764), Robert Clive concluded the Treaty of Allahabad with Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II on 16 August 1765.]

Q3. The Northern Circars of Andhra Pradesh were formally ceded to the British East India Company by which Nizam of Hyderabad in 1766?
(a) Asaf Jah I
(b) Nasir Jung
(c) Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II)
(d) Mir Mahbub Ali Khan
Correct Answer: (c) Nizam Ali Khan (Asaf Jah II) [Explanation: In 1766, Nizam Ali Khan signed a treaty with the EIC at Hyderabad ceding the Northern Circars in return for British military assistance.]

Q4. In which year was the historic Regulation XVII declaring the practice of Sati illegal and punishable as culpable homicide enacted by Lord William Bentinck?
(a) 1813
(b) 1829
(c) 1833
(d) 1856
Correct Answer: (b) 1829 [Explanation: Through the relentless efforts of Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Lord William Bentinck promulgated the Bengal Sati Regulation on 4 December 1829.]

Q5. Which British Viceroy is revered as the 'Father of Local Self-Government in India' for his landmark Resolution of 1882 establishing rural and municipal local boards?
(a) Lord Lytton
(b) Lord Ripon
(c) Lord Curzon
(d) Lord Dufferin
Correct Answer: (b) Lord Ripon [Explanation: Lord Ripon's Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882 laid the foundation of representative municipal and local administration in British India.]
